title: How I Architected My Astro Portfolio Beyond Pages and Components
excerpt: A practical case study of Folio X: how content contracts, page composition, Project patterns, Components, Layouts, and progressive enhancement create clear ownership in a growing Astro portfolio.
author: Nguyễn Kim Thu
imageAlt: Layered Astro portfolio architecture showing content, page composition, Project patterns, Components and Layouts connected through explicit ownership boundaries
content:
When I started Folio X, the architecture problem looked ordinary: build a portfolio with Astro, keep the code reusable, and make the content easy to maintain. That is usually where advice stops — create pages, extract components, and keep files small.

That approach works for a small site. It becomes less useful when the same codebase has to support project pages, product archives, blog posts, publication readers, filters, galleries, sidebars, reusable card collections, CMS-managed data, and optional client-side behavior without turning every route into a custom implementation.

The architecture I use now is built around one question: which layer owns this responsibility? Content owns data. Page composition owns how content becomes page regions. Project patterns own reusable product-level behavior. Components render smaller UI units. Layouts own structural geometry. Scripts progressively enhance the HTML only when a feature actually exists on the page.

This article explains that structure from the current Folio X source rather than presenting a generic Astro folder recipe. The goal is not to prove that one folder tree is universally correct. The goal is to show how explicit ownership helped me keep a growing portfolio understandable while still allowing the design and content model to evolve.

Why “pages and components” were not enough

A common frontend structure has two obvious levels: route files and reusable components. At first, that is enough. A route composes a hero, cards, text, and a footer. Repeated pieces become components.

The problem appears when reuse is no longer the hardest question.

Consider five different pages in the same site:

  • a project detail page with editorial content and related work;
  • a product archive with filters, sorting, pagination, and multiple card views;
  • a blog article with author metadata and a table of contents;
  • a publication reader with reader-specific controls;
  • a home page that combines several collection types.

All of them can reuse buttons, headings, cards, and containers, but that does not answer who owns the page structure, who resolves CMS data, who controls collection loops, or where optional JavaScript belongs.

If every route solves those problems independently, route files gradually become a second design system. If the CMS can select arbitrary components and arbitrary classes, the CMS becomes the design system. If low-level components start reading route state or business data, those components stop being reusable in any meaningful sense.

So I stopped treating architecture mainly as a question of file size and started treating it as a question of ownership.

The architecture in one view

The current Folio X flow is easier to understand as a sequence of contracts:

The important part of this map is the direction of dependency. Higher-level layers are allowed to depend on lower-level rendering layers. Lower-level layers do not reach upward to decide page structure, CMS behavior, or business context.

That creates a practical rule I can use while implementing features:

  • if a decision describes content, it belongs in the content contract;
  • if it converts content into application props, it belongs in page composition or data mapping;
  • if it owns a reusable product-level pattern or collection behavior, it belongs in P*;
  • if it renders one smaller UI unit, it belongs in C*;
  • if it controls page geometry, sections, containers, or sidebars, it belongs in L*;
  • if it enhances already useful HTML, it belongs in a feature script.

Content is a contract, not a component picker

Folio X uses structured content and schemas so that page data enters the application in a predictable shape. A page can contain metadata, SEO data, a layout template, and approved sections. A blog entry can contain article metadata and a single article body. Product, project, publication, and other collections have their own contracts.

The important design choice is what the CMS is not allowed to do. It does not store an arbitrary Astro component path. It does not decide which implementation file should render a region. It does not need to know Tailwind class names.

Instead, CMS values stay inside a vocabulary the application already understands. For page layouts, that means approved layout keys. For collection presentation, that means approved options that page composition can map to a known Project contract.

This separation matters because CMS flexibility has a cost. Every arbitrary presentation value becomes a public data contract that future code must continue to understand. A completely free-form page builder can feel powerful during the first few pages and expensive after dozens of entries depend on old implementation details.

Why I map CMS values before rendering

The page builder acts as an adapter between CMS-facing data and application-facing props. That means a content value can remain editorially meaningful while code maps it to a concrete implementation.

For example, a CMS may describe a collection layout using an approved value such as carousel. The application can map that value to the PCard collection template that implements slider behavior. The content entry does not import a slider and does not need to know its folder path.

This gives both sides a stable responsibility:

LayerResponsibility
CMS/contentDescribe content and approved editorial choices
Page compositionNormalize those choices into application contracts
Project patternOwn reusable product-level structure and behavior
ComponentRender smaller UI contracts
LayoutOwn structural geometry and page framing

Page composition is the boundary between data and UI

The page composition layer lives under src/components/pages/. Its job is not to reproduce every DOM element a page needs. Its job is to turn page data into the typed contracts used by the Project layer.

The home page demonstrates this clearly. HomePage.astro is intentionally small: it loads page data and passes that data into PageBuilder. The page builder resolves collection sources, section settings, archive behavior, card presentations, and page regions.

This keeps route-level and page-level composition focused. They do not need to know how one card renders metadata, how a gallery manages thumbnails, or how the product archive script filters DOM nodes.

Why PageBuilder can be large without owning the DOM

PageBuilder.astro contains a substantial amount of mapping logic. That is intentional because it is the adapter between different data contracts. Size alone is not the architecture smell I care about.

The more important question is whether the file owns responsibilities that should belong somewhere else. In the current structure, the builder resolves data and constructs props, but the final DOM for reusable patterns still belongs to those patterns.

For a sourced collection, the builder may resolve items from products, projects, labs, blog posts, comics, novels, or publications. It then constructs the PCard configuration and passes the actual collection to the card pattern. The builder does not duplicate the item rendering loop for every page.

PPage owns page-template selection

After page data has been normalized into regions, PPage owns page-template dispatch.

The current source supports these structural page templates:

  • stacked;
  • lead-content;
  • lead-content-closing;
  • lead-content-navigation;
  • lead-navigation-content.

PPage receives the selected template and the normalized regions. It selects the corresponding structural template, places it inside LPage, and passes the regions down.

That is a deliberately narrow responsibility. PPage does not decide how a card works. It does not know how a blog article body is rendered. It does not fetch CMS data. It answers one structural question: which approved page composition should arrange these regions?

Page templates own order and section framing

A page template such as PageLeadContent can identify lead regions, order the remaining content, and decide how each region is framed by LSection.

The existing section: false contract is a small example of why ownership matters. If a region already belongs to a larger structural composition, it can render without an extra section wrapper. The template owns that framing decision instead of forcing every region into the same wrapper.

That rule came from inspecting the actual DOM and correcting unnecessary nesting. Architecture has to survive the rendered HTML, not only look tidy in a directory tree.

PageRegionContent is a typed region dispatcher

Once a page template has decided where a region belongs, PageRegionContent decides which Project or Component contract renders it.

The region union includes page headers, heroes, articles, reviews, cards, CTAs, collections, archives, status blocks, tabs, galleries, entry indexes, readers, detail lists, profiles, tables of contents, advertisements, and groups.

The key point is that the region is discriminated and typed. A region with component: "article" carries PArticleProps. A card region carries PCardProps. A gallery region carries PGalleryProps.

This avoids a pattern I wanted to stay away from: a generic component name plus Record<string, unknown> props. That kind of generic dispatcher is flexible, but the type system can no longer tell whether the CMS data actually matches the component contract.

Group regions handle composition without inventing a new layer

The group region can separate nested regions into main and aside placements. When aside regions exist, the dispatcher composes them through LSidebar; otherwise it renders the main group directly.

This allows editorial pages to combine an article, author information, TOC, related content, or other patterns without creating a new one-off layout class for every page type.

The group is still constrained by the same approved region union. It is composition, not an unlimited recursive visual-programming system.

Project patterns own reusable product-level behavior

The P* layer is where Folio X places reusable patterns that are larger than a small component but smaller than a full page.

Examples include cards, galleries, archives, page headers, readers, filters, CTAs, advertisements, post navigation, reviews, and status patterns.

A Project pattern is allowed to own control flow when that control flow is part of the pattern’s responsibility. This is important because “do not put loops in components” is too simplistic to be useful.

If a card collection is the responsibility of PCard, then PCard should own the collection loop. A page composition layer should not repeat the same mapping logic every time a card collection appears. The selected single-card renderer should render one item and should not secretly own the collection.

This is the topic of the next article in the series: Component Ownership: Where Should the Loop Actually Live?

Components render smaller UI contracts

The C* layer contains smaller reusable units such as buttons, links, headings, images, metadata, rows, columns, tags, tabs, progress indicators, selects, and the single-item card renderer.

The rule I try to preserve is that a Component should not need to know which page it appears on.

A button should not inspect the current route to decide its business meaning. A metadata item should not fetch its own content. An image should not know whether it belongs to a product detail page or a blog card. A single card should not decide the layout of the collection that contains it.

This keeps context flowing downward as props instead of being rediscovered inside low-level UI.

Layouts own geometry

The L* layer owns structural geometry: page framing, section framing, containers, sidebars, spacing relationships, and similar layout concerns.

This gives the rest of the component system somewhere to delegate geometry instead of scattering page-width and section-spacing decisions throughout Project patterns.

It also improves audits. If a page feels too wide or a sidebar collapses incorrectly, I can begin with the layout owner instead of searching every feature pattern for duplicated width utilities.

Tailwind remains the styling standard in Folio X. I do not treat every utility combination as something that must be promoted into a custom token. The architectural concern is not eliminating Tailwind classes; it is making sure layout decisions are owned by the layer responsible for layout.

Progressive enhancement keeps JavaScript feature-specific

Astro renders HTML without requiring a client-side application runtime for ordinary components. I wanted Folio X to keep that property even as the site gained interactive features.

The site has a central main.ts, but feature scripts are imported conditionally based on the DOM.

  • image-gallery logic is loaded only when an image gallery exists;
  • article TOC logic is loaded only when an article TOC exists;
  • archive filtering is loaded only on archive pages that need it;
  • collection filtering is loaded only when the matching root exists;
  • product filtering logic is loaded only for faceted product results;
  • reader behavior is loaded only for reader pages;
  • slider behavior is loaded only when a slider is present.

Core site-wide behaviors remain statically initialized because they can reasonably exist across the site. Feature-specific behaviors stay conditional.

The result is a practical form of progressive enhancement: useful HTML is the base, and JavaScript adds behavior to pages that need it.

The dependency direction I try to preserve

The architecture is easiest to maintain when dependencies mostly move downward:

CMS / content
      ↓
schemas and data contracts
      ↓
page composition / mapping
      ↓
PPage + typed regions
      ↓
Project patterns
      ↓
Components + Layouts
      ↓
HTML
      ↓
optional feature scripts

This is not a strict academic clean-architecture implementation. It is a practical frontend rule.

A lower layer should not need to reach back into the CMS to understand itself. A layout should not import a page-specific mapper. A card item renderer should not decide which archive page it belongs to. A page builder is allowed to know about Project contracts because adapting page data into Project props is exactly its job.

What this architecture costs

The main cost is explicitness.

A feature may require a type, a variant mapping, a template, a page-region contract, or a mapper change instead of one large component with many conditional props. There are more named boundaries to understand.

That trade-off only makes sense if those boundaries carry real ownership. Creating extra files because a convention says “every component needs five files” would only produce ceremony.

The value appears when the same patterns are reused across different pages. A card collection can change without rewriting every route. A page template can change its composition without teaching cards about page layout. CMS values can evolve through a mapper without exposing internal implementation details to content entries.

The danger is over-abstraction

The opposite failure mode is also possible. If every two-line pattern becomes a dispatcher, every style becomes a variant object, and every page needs multiple abstraction layers, architecture starts hiding the product instead of clarifying it.

I use two checks before extracting a new architectural unit:

  1. Does this unit own a responsibility that already appears more than once?
  2. Would putting this responsibility in an existing layer make that layer own something it should not own?

If the answer to both is no, I usually keep the implementation simpler.

How I decide where a new feature belongs

When adding a feature, I now work from ownership before choosing a folder.

1. Identify the business or editorial contract

What information actually needs to be stored? Which values are meaningful to an editor or data source? Which values are only implementation details?

2. Decide who owns the control flow

If it is a repeated collection, which pattern owns that collection? If it is page ordering, which page template owns it? If it is one UI item, the item renderer should not inherit collection responsibilities.

3. Keep layout separate from content meaning

A section may need a container, spacing, or sidebar. Those are structural concerns and should be handled by the layout/composition system instead of being encoded into article text or low-level components.

4. Add JavaScript only where the HTML needs enhancement

If the feature can render useful HTML first, I keep that as the base. The script should attach to an explicit DOM contract rather than recreate the entire page as client state.

5. Check the rendered DOM, not only the source tree

Architecture can look elegant in TypeScript and still produce duplicate wrappers, incorrect heading hierarchy, broken focus order, or redundant collection markup. Source organization is only one part of frontend architecture.

What made the architecture better over time

Folio X did not arrive at this structure in one design session. Some boundaries only became obvious after implementing real pages and auditing the results.

One example is card ownership. The system now separates the collection-level PCard responsibility from the single-item CCard renderer. Another is page sections: the current templates explicitly support section: false when an extra semantic wrapper is not appropriate. Feature scripts were also moved toward conditional imports instead of being treated as one global bundle of behavior.

Those changes share the same pattern: when a layer starts owning two different reasons to change, split the responsibility at the boundary that is actually causing the problem.

What I would keep if I rebuilt Folio X

I would keep five decisions.

  1. Typed content contracts. Content should be validated before it reaches rendering code.
  2. A page-composition adapter. CMS-facing values should be translated into application contracts instead of leaking directly into component APIs.
  3. Explicit ownership for collection patterns. Repeated control flow should live with the pattern that owns the collection.
  4. Layouts as first-class structural primitives. Geometry should not be reinvented inside every feature.
  5. HTML first, behavior second. Feature JavaScript should enhance the page instead of becoming the page unless the feature truly requires an application runtime.

I would also keep one warning: do not copy this folder structure only because it exists. The useful part is the reasoning behind the boundaries. A smaller project should use fewer layers. A different product may need different owners.

The main lesson: architecture is ownership

The most useful change in Folio X was not introducing more folders. It was being able to answer questions like these consistently:

  • Who owns this collection loop?
  • Who translates this CMS value?
  • Who decides whether a section wrapper exists?
  • Who owns the sidebar geometry?
  • Who renders one item?
  • Who loads the feature script?

Once those answers are explicit, the codebase becomes easier to change because each modification has a natural place to start.

This is the same systems-thinking principle behind my previous case study, E-commerce Promotion Automation: From 8 Hours to 15 Minutes. In that project, the important improvement came from deciding where a business operation should be owned before automating it. In Folio X, the same idea applies to frontend responsibilities.

The next article will narrow the scope to one concrete example: Component Ownership: Where Should the Loop Actually Live? It will use the current PCard and CCard separation to show why iteration is not just syntax — it is an architectural responsibility.
